title: Debugging Strategies
tagline: Apply the scientific method to bugs: reproduce, hypothesise, isolate, fix — using breakpoints, logging, bisection, and rubber duck debugging.

sections.content:
Every programmer debugs. The difference between a junior and a senior developer is not that seniors write bug-free code — it is that seniors have **systematic strategies** that find and fix bugs faster, regardless of language, domain, or codebase size. Senior engineers have internalized a mental toolkit: a set of reliable moves they reach for automatically when something goes wrong.

Debugging is fundamentally the **scientific method applied to code**: observe a symptom, form a hypothesis about the cause, design an experiment that would falsify that hypothesis, run it, and update your model based on the result. This sounds simple, but most debugging mistakes share a common root — skipping one of these steps. Engineers jump to hypotheses before reproducing the bug reliably. They run experiments that cannot distinguish between causes. They fix a symptom and declare victory without confirming the root cause is gone. Systematic debugging eliminates these shortcuts.

The cardinal rule of all debugging is **reproduce the bug first**. You cannot fix what you cannot reliably trigger. Once you have a consistent reproduction, the problem becomes a matter of progressively **narrowing the search space**: is the bug in the frontend or backend? In this module or the one calling it? In the current code or a dependency? Before this week's commits or after? Every debugging technique is just a more or less efficient way of answering that question.

This chapter covers the full toolkit: the scientific loop, bisection and `git bisect`, rubber duck debugging and why it works, breakpoints and the step debugger, structured logging for production, defensive programming with assertions and guard clauses, and the discipline of writing regression tests so each bug you fix becomes a permanent safety check. These techniques compose — a senior engineer weaves them together fluidly, choosing the cheapest experiment that will eliminate the most uncertainty.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    OBS["Observe Symptom\n(wrong output / crash / silence)"]
    REPR["Reproduce Reliably\n(minimal failing case)"]
    HYP["Form Hypothesis\n(specific suspected cause)"]
    EXP["Design Experiment\n(breakpoint / log / test / bisect)"]
    RUN["Run Experiment"]
    CONF["Hypothesis Confirmed?"]
    FIX["Apply Fix"]
    VER["Verify Fix + Write Regression Test"]
    NEW["Refine / New Hypothesis"]
    OBS --> REPR
    REPR --> HYP
    HYP --> EXP
    EXP --> RUN
    RUN --> CONF
    CONF -->|"yes"| FIX
    CONF -->|"no"| NEW
    NEW --> HYP
    FIX --> VER
sections.caption: The scientific debugging loop. Each iteration narrows the search space. The loop always ends in a regression test — not just a fix — so the bug cannot silently resurface.

sections.title: The Doctor's Differential Diagnosis
sections.content:
A skilled physician does not randomly prescribe medication when a patient arrives with a headache. They take a **patient history** (when did it start? what makes it worse? any other symptoms?), then **examine the patient directly** (blood pressure, pupil response, neck stiffness), then form a **differential diagnosis** — a ranked list of candidate causes ordered by probability — then order **targeted tests** that can rule out each candidate efficiently, and finally update the diagnosis based on each test result.

Every step of that clinical process maps directly to software debugging. **Reproduce first** is taking the patient's temperature: without reliable data, every guess is noise. The **differential diagnosis** is your hypothesis list — not 'the bug is somewhere in the app' but 'the most likely cause is a null user object, second most likely is a race condition in the async callback, third is a bad API response'. **Bisection** (binary search through commits or code) is like ordering a lab panel that rules out entire organ systems at once: not liver → not kidney → must be cardiac. The **step debugger** is the stethoscope: it lets you listen to the program's internal state at a precise moment in time rather than inferring it from external symptoms alone. And **rubber duck debugging** is explaining the case to a colleague before rounds — the act of articulating forces assumptions to the surface.

What distinguishes expert debuggers is that they maintain this discipline even under pressure. When production is down and everyone is watching, the temptation is to start changing things at random hoping something fixes it. This is the equivalent of a panicking doctor administering every drug in the cabinet. The scientific loop is slower for the first five minutes and dramatically faster for everything after.

sections.title: Reproduce First: Building the Minimal Failing Case
sections.content:
The most common debugging mistake is attempting to fix a bug before you can reliably trigger it. Without a consistent reproduction you have no way to know whether your fix actually worked, or whether the bug just did not happen to manifest on that particular run.

**The goal is the minimal failing case**: the smallest, most isolated input or sequence of steps that reliably triggers the wrong behavior. Strip out unrelated code. Replace network calls with hardcoded responses. Use the simplest possible data. The process of building the minimal case frequently reveals the bug on its own — you discover that the bug disappears when you remove feature X, which tells you the bug is in feature X.

A minimal reproduction also has a second major benefit: it is easy to share. If you need to ask a colleague for help, or file a bug report on an open-source dependency, a twelve-line script that always reproduces the problem is infinitely more useful than 'it breaks when I do some stuff in the app under certain conditions'.

**What counts as reproduced?** Ideally, the bug fires on every single run. If it is intermittent — a race condition, a flaky network response, a timing-dependent crash — you need a slightly different strategy: identify under what conditions it fires more or less frequently, then construct a test harness that increases frequency (running the scenario in a tight loop, injecting artificial latency, using a mock clock). An intermittent bug that fires 10% of the time can be made to fire 10 times per second with the right harness, which is effectively deterministic.

**Isolate the environment.** A bug that only appears on one developer's machine might be a version mismatch, a different OS path separator, a different locale, or a different time zone. Compare environment variables, dependency versions (run `node --version`, `python --version`, check `package-lock.json` or `requirements.txt`), and OS settings. Docker is invaluable here — packaging the exact environment makes 'works on my machine' an eliminable variable.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    FULL["Full application\n(800+ files)"]
    MOD["Suspicious module\n(one file)"]
    FUNC["Suspicious function\n(one function)"]
    CASE["Minimal input\n(3 lines)"]
    FULL -->|"remove unrelated code"| MOD
    MOD -->|"remove unrelated functions"| FUNC
    FUNC -->|"hardcode minimal input"| CASE
sections.caption: Shrink the reproduction surface until only the essential behavior remains. Each reduction step makes the root cause more visible.

sections.title: The Scientific Method: Falsifiable Hypotheses and Controlled Experiments
sections.content:
Once you can reproduce the bug, form a **specific, falsifiable hypothesis**. 'Something is wrong with the payment flow' is not a hypothesis — it is a restatement of the symptom. A real hypothesis looks like: 'The cart total is wrong because `qty` arrives as a string from the API and string multiplication in JavaScript produces NaN or string concatenation instead of numeric multiplication.'

A falsifiable hypothesis is one you can *prove wrong*. If your experiment can only confirm the hypothesis but never refute it, the experiment is not useful. The best experiments are the ones where you can predict exactly what will happen under both the 'hypothesis is correct' and 'hypothesis is incorrect' cases:

- If `qty` is a string, then `console.log(typeof item.qty)` will print `'string'`.
- If `qty` is a number, it will print `'number'`.

Run the experiment. If the output is `'string'`, your hypothesis is confirmed and you know the fix (coerce with `Number()`). If it is `'number'`, your hypothesis is wrong, you have eliminated one cause, and you form a new hypothesis.

**The golden rule of experiments: change one thing at a time.** If you change three things simultaneously and the bug disappears, you do not know which change fixed it. You might remove the wrong two changes and reintroduce the bug. Worse, two of the changes might have been harmless or even counterproductive, and you now ship unnecessary code changes. In a collaborative codebase, unnecessary changes create merge conflicts and add cognitive load for reviewers.

**Maintain a debugging log.** When a bug takes more than fifteen minutes to resolve, write down what you have tried and what the results were. This prevents the frustrating experience of trying the same experiment twice an hour later because you forgot you already ruled it out. It also gives you a narrative to share with a colleague if you get stuck.

sections.title: Bisection: Binary Search Through Commits and Code
sections.content:
**Bisection** is the most powerful technique for a specific class of bugs: regressions, where something used to work and now does not. The insight is that commit history is a sorted array — sorted by time — and you can binary-search through it to find the first commit that introduced the bug in O(log n) steps instead of O(n).

With `git bisect`, you tell Git the last known-good commit and the current known-bad commit. Git checks out the midpoint commit. You test it (run your minimal reproduction case). You mark it `good` or `bad`. Git checks out the new midpoint. Repeat. After log₂(n) rounds, Git identifies the exact commit that introduced the regression. For a project with 1000 commits between good and bad, this takes at most 10 rounds — each round costs only the time to run your test.

The workflow:
```
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v2.1.0
# Git checks out a midpoint commit
# ... run your test ...
git bisect good   # or: git bisect bad
# Git checks out the new midpoint
# ... repeat until Git prints: 'abc123 is the first bad commit'
git bisect reset  # return to HEAD
```

If you have an automated test for the bug, you can fully automate bisect: `git bisect run yarn test --testNamePattern='cart total'`. Git will run the command at each midpoint and use the exit code (0 = good, non-zero = bad) to navigate automatically.

**The same bisection logic applies within code.** If you have a multi-step pipeline — parse → validate → transform → render — and the output is wrong, you do not need to read all four steps. Add a log or assertion at the midpoint (after step 2). If the intermediate state is correct there, the bug is in step 3 or 4; if wrong, it is in step 1 or 2. Apply recursively until isolated to a single function or even a single line. This is dramatically faster than reading the entire pipeline top-to-bottom hoping to spot the error by eye.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant DEV as Developer
    participant GIT as git bisect
    participant TEST as Test Script
    DEV->>GIT: git bisect start
    DEV->>GIT: git bisect bad HEAD
    DEV->>GIT: git bisect good v1.0
    GIT-->>DEV: Checkout commit at midpoint M1
    DEV->>TEST: Run test
    TEST-->>DEV: FAIL
    DEV->>GIT: git bisect bad
    GIT-->>DEV: Checkout earlier midpoint M2
    DEV->>TEST: Run test
    TEST-->>DEV: PASS
    DEV->>GIT: git bisect good
    GIT-->>DEV: Found first bad commit
sections.caption: git bisect performs binary search over commits. Each good/bad label halves the search space. 1024 commits → found in exactly 10 steps.

sections.title: Rubber Duck Debugging: The Power of Articulation
sections.content:
Rubber duck debugging is the practice of explaining your code, line by line, out loud to an inanimate object — a rubber duck, a potted plant, a blank document, or an imaginary colleague. The technique was popularized in the book *The Pragmatic Programmer* by Hunt and Thomas, though programmers had been practicing it informally long before.

Why does it work? When you *write* code, your brain operates in execution mode — it knows what you *intended* each line to do, and it fills in that intent automatically when you re-read the code. The intention and the implementation blur together. When you *explain* code to someone else (even an inanimate proxy), you have to translate it into language: you have to make the implicit explicit. This forces a different kind of processing — a meta-cognitive layer on top of the code.

The moment you say 'and here I assume the user object always has a `name` property,' you hear yourself say the word 'assume,' and a small alarm fires. *Do I actually know that? Have I verified it? What happens when it is null?* The contradiction between what you believe and what the code actually does surfaces in the act of articulation.

Rubber duck debugging is particularly effective for two categories of bugs:

1. **Logic errors** — where the code does exactly what you wrote, but what you wrote is not what you meant. Explaining 'and then I multiply price by qty' when qty is a string immediately surfaces the type mismatch.

2. **Assumption violations** — where you made an implicit assumption (this array is never empty, this callback always fires exactly once, this API returns UTC times) that turned out to be false. Stating assumptions explicitly is the first step to questioning them.

A structured rubber duck checklist for when you are stuck: (1) What does this function receive — type, range, can it be null or undefined? (2) What does it return, and when? (3) What are the side effects — does it mutate shared state, write to disk, call an API? (4) What has already been verified to work? (5) What is the first line where 'correct' becomes 'incorrect'? Answering question 5 specifically reduces the problem to a single-line suspect.

sections.title: Breakpoints and the Step Debugger
sections.content:
A **breakpoint** is an instruction to the runtime to pause execution at a specific line and transfer control to the debugger, letting you inspect the program's full state — all in-scope variables, the call stack, heap objects — at that exact moment. This is categorically more powerful than `console.log` for interactive debugging because:

- You can inspect any variable without knowing in advance which ones matter.
- You can evaluate arbitrary expressions in the debugger's console against the live program state.
- You can see the full call stack — not just the current function, but the entire chain of calls that led here.
- You can modify variable values in-flight and resume execution to test hypotheses without restarting.

**Breakpoint types** beyond the basic line breakpoint:

- **Conditional breakpoints**: pause only when a condition is true (e.g., `item.id === 42`). Essential for loops with thousands of iterations.
- **Logpoints** (VS Code): print a message without pausing, like a non-intrusive `console.log` that you can add and remove without touching code.
- **Exception breakpoints**: pause automatically whenever any exception is thrown, even if caught. Catches bugs that swallow errors silently.
- **Watch expressions**: continuously evaluate an expression as you step, alerting you when it changes.

**Stepping commands** in any debugger:
- **Step Over (F10)**: execute the current line and pause at the next line in the same function. If the line contains a function call, the entire function runs without entering it.
- **Step Into (F11)**: descend into the function being called on the current line.
- **Step Out (Shift+F11)**: run the rest of the current function and pause at the caller.
- **Continue (F5)**: run until the next breakpoint.

**Strategy for using the step debugger efficiently**: do not start at line 1 and step through everything. Set a breakpoint just before the point where the output first looks wrong, confirm the inputs are what you expected, then step through the suspicious logic. Use Step Over for functions you trust, Step Into only when you need to verify a function's internal behavior.

sections.explanation: The minimal reproduction immediately surfaces the string-qty bug without reading any surrounding code. The guard clause converts a silent NaN into an explicit error message that names the exact item causing the problem. The regression tests encode the fix permanently — any future change that reintroduces the bug will fail the 'string qty' test immediately.

sections.title: Structured Logging for Production Debugging
sections.content:
When a production system is misbehaving, you typically cannot attach a debugger. The application is running on a remote server, handling real user traffic, and pausing execution for inspection is not an option. This is where **structured logging** becomes your primary debugging tool.

Structured logging means emitting log entries as machine-parseable records (usually JSON or key-value pairs) rather than free-form strings. Each entry includes: a timestamp, a severity level, the message, and a structured data payload with all the context needed to understand the entry without reading surrounding lines.

**Log levels** correspond to urgency and verbosity:
- `DEBUG`: detailed trace information, inputs and outputs of individual functions. Too verbose for production; invaluable when troubleshooting.
- `INFO`: normal operational events — 'order processed', 'user logged in'. Fine for production.
- `WARN`: unexpected but recoverable — 'cache miss, falling through to DB', 'deprecated API called'. Investigate these when they spike.
- `ERROR`: a specific operation failed — 'payment processing failed for order 42'. Requires investigation.
- `FATAL`/`CRITICAL`: the system cannot continue — 'database connection pool exhausted'. Pages the on-call engineer.

**What to log**: at a minimum, log at function entry with inputs (or a summary of inputs) and at function exit with the output or result status. Log every external call (HTTP, database, queue) with its duration and outcome. Log every state transition (order moved to 'processing', user account locked). Never log sensitive data — passwords, full credit card numbers, auth tokens.

**Correlation IDs** are essential in distributed systems. When a single user request fans out across multiple services, you need a way to find all the log entries belonging to that request. Generate a unique ID at the edge (the API gateway or the first service) and propagate it through every downstream call in the request headers. Log it on every entry. Then finding all logs for a failing request is a single filter query.

**Log aggregation tools** — Datadog, Grafana Loki, ELK Stack (Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana), AWS CloudWatch Logs Insights — let you search, filter, and aggregate logs across all your service instances. Learning to write effective queries in your log tool is as important as knowing how to write the logs in the first place.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Every log entry carries the correlationId, so filtering your log aggregation tool by a single ID shows the complete lifecycle of any request across all services. The level system lets you enable debug output temporarily in staging without changing code, by setting the LOG_LEVEL environment variable.

sections.title: Defensive Programming: Assertions and Guard Clauses
sections.content:
Most bugs are caused by a violation of an implicit assumption: a function receives data it was not designed to handle, a variable holds a value the programmer did not expect, or a subsystem behaves differently than assumed. **Defensive programming** is the practice of making these assumptions explicit and executable, so that violations produce loud, informative errors rather than silent wrong behavior.

**Guard clauses** at function entry check preconditions before any work is done. Instead of letting a null propagate through five function calls until it eventually causes a cryptic 'Cannot read property of undefined' error at line 342 of an unrelated function, a guard clause catches it immediately at the point of entry and emits an error message that names exactly what was missing and where.

**`console.assert(condition, message)`** is a lightweight way to document assumptions inline. It prints the message to the console only when the condition is false. Unlike a thrown exception, it does not halt execution by default, making it appropriate for development-time sanity checks that should never fire in correct code. In production builds, you can strip them out or leave them in — they are silent when correct.

**Fail fast, fail loudly.** The principle of failing fast says: when something is wrong, produce an error immediately and close to the source, rather than propagating the wrong state until it causes a confusing failure far away. This principle is why TypeScript's strict null checks are valuable: they fail at compile time rather than at runtime in production.

**Design by contract** (popularized by Eiffel and later Clojure's `:pre`/`:post` conditions) formalizes this idea: every function specifies its preconditions (what must be true of the inputs), postconditions (what will be true of the output), and invariants (what must remain true of the object's state). Even without formal tooling, documenting these in comments and checking them with guards makes a codebase dramatically easier to debug.

**The real value of assertions** is not catching bugs at runtime — it is narrowing the search space during debugging. When a function with explicit guards fails, the error message tells you exactly which assumption was violated and in what call context. Compare these two error messages:

- Without guard: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'trim')` at line 247 of `formatUserName.js`
- With guard: `Error: getUsername: user is required` at line 3 of `getUsername.js`

The second tells you the caller passed null or undefined, where to look, and what to fix. The first requires tracing back through the call stack to discover what was null and why.

flowchart TD
    CALL["Caller passes null user"]
    NOGUARD["No Guard Clause"]
    DEEP["Error 5 calls deep:\nCannot read property trim"]
    GUARD["Guard Clause at Entry"]
    EARLY["Immediate Error:\ngetUsername: user required"]
    CALL --> NOGUARD
    CALL --> GUARD
    NOGUARD --> DEEP
    GUARD --> EARLY
    DEEP -->|"requires stack trace analysis"| ROOT["Root: caller passed null"]
    EARLY -->|"error message names the cause"| ROOT
sections.caption: Without a guard clause, a null propagates through the call stack and surfaces as a cryptic error far from its origin. A guard clause catches it immediately with a descriptive message.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Guard clauses at function entry convert downstream cryptic errors into immediate, named failures. The binary search checkpoint pattern (an assertion at the midpoint of a pipeline) quickly identifies which half of the code contains the bug, cutting investigation time in half with each checkpoint.

sections.title: Common Debugging Traps and Misconceptions
sections.content:
**The Heisenbug**: a bug that disappears when you try to observe it. Adding a `console.log` statement changes timing, which fixes a race condition. Running the test suite slowly (because the debugger is attached) eliminates a timeout bug. The observation itself alters the behavior. Heisenbugs are almost always caused by timing-dependent code — concurrent operations, timeouts, or event ordering. Fix strategy: use logging that does not alter timing (write-only side channel), use deterministic mocks for timers, or use tools specifically designed for concurrent debugging like thread sanitizers.

**The Scapegoat Commit**: blaming the most recent commit because that is the last thing that changed, when the bug was actually latent for months and the recent commit merely changed the conditions that exposed it. Always let bisect identify the causal commit rather than assuming recency implies causality.

**Fixing the symptom instead of the root cause**: adding a null-check around the crash without asking why the value was null in the first place. The null-check stops the crash but the upstream problem — the API returning null when it should not, or the calling code failing to handle an error — remains. Three months later it causes a different crash in a different place. Always trace symptoms back to root causes.

**Tunnel vision**: spending two hours debugging one theory when a fresh pair of eyes would have spotted the real cause in two minutes. Recognise the signs — you are re-reading the same five lines repeatedly and each time you expect them to be different. When this happens, take a five-minute break, explain the bug to someone else (rubber duck if no one is available), or start fresh from the reproduction rather than from your current state of mind.

**Undefined behavior and environment differences**: a bug that only appears on Linux, or only in Node 18, or only under load, or only when a specific environment variable is set. Always include environment details in bug reports. Always test fixes in the same environment where the bug appears. Container tooling (Docker) is the best solution to environment-difference bugs because it makes 'the environment' explicit and reproducible.

**Silent failures**: when an error is swallowed by a bare `catch {}` block, or a Promise rejection is not handled, or a failing callback is ignored. These produce mysterious wrong state with no error message. Audit your codebase for empty catch blocks, ensure all Promise chains have `.catch()` or `try/catch`, and use Node's `process.on('unhandledRejection')` or equivalent to surface these failures.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    SYMPTOM["Symptom: crash at line 247"]
    IMMEDIATE["Immediate Cause: null user"]
    ROOT["Root Cause: API returns null on 404"]
    FIX_WRONG["Wrong Fix: add null check at line 247"]
    FIX_RIGHT["Right Fix: handle 404 at API call site"]
    SYMPTOM --> IMMEDIATE
    IMMEDIATE --> ROOT
    SYMPTOM --> FIX_WRONG
    ROOT --> FIX_RIGHT
    FIX_WRONG -->|"latent bug remains"| FUTURE["Future crash elsewhere"]
    FIX_RIGHT -->|"root cause eliminated"| SAFE["Bug cannot recur"]
sections.caption: Always trace symptoms back to root causes. Fixing only the crash site leaves the underlying bad state intact, guaranteeing a future symptom in a different location.

sections.title: Regression Tests: Converting Bugs Into Permanent Safety Checks
sections.content:
After you find and fix a bug, the final — and often skipped — step is writing a **regression test**: a test whose purpose is to verify that the specific bug does not recur. The test encodes the minimal reproduction case as an automated check that runs on every future commit.

The value of a regression test is not in catching the bug the first time (you already did that manually). The value is in the second, third, and fourth times — months later, after a refactoring that touches the relevant code, after a dependency upgrade that changes behavior, after a new developer adds a feature and unknowingly reintroduces the old pattern. Without the test, the bug silently reappears in production. With the test, it fails loudly and immediately in CI, costs nothing to identify, and is fixed in minutes because the test tells you exactly what broke.

The naming convention for regression tests should make the original bug traceable: `test('cart total: string qty should be coerced to number — bug #1234')`. When this test fails two years later, the developer sees immediately which bug is being recurred, can read the original ticket for context, and understands the expected fix.

**Mutation testing** is a technique that validates whether your tests are actually useful: automated tools make small changes (mutations) to your source code — flipping a `>` to `>=`, changing a `+` to a `-`, deleting a guard clause — and check whether any of your tests fail. If a mutation does not fail any test, that portion of code is insufficiently tested. Mutation testing is expensive but powerful for auditing test suite quality.

The broader discipline is **test-driven debugging** (TDD for bugs): before writing any fix, write the failing test that demonstrates the bug. Confirm the test fails in the expected way (the wrong output, not just 'test error'). Then write the fix. Confirm the test passes. Then ensure no other tests regressed. This sequence proves the fix works, proves the test is meaningful, and leaves the test in place permanently.

**Historical context**: The word 'bug' for a software defect was popularized by Grace Hopper's team in 1947 when they taped an actual moth that had short-circuited a relay in the Harvard Mark II computer into their logbook, annotating it 'first actual case of bug being found.' But the term predates computing — Thomas Edison used 'bug' in 1878 to describe faults in his electrical designs. The practice of systematic debugging also has deep roots: the scientific method formalized by Francis Bacon in the 1600s, and the hypothesis-experiment cycle that underlies it, is precisely the same loop good debuggers use today.

**Interview and production war-story traps to know:**

- **'Change one thing at a time'** is the rule most often violated under pressure. Examiners test this by describing a scenario where two changes were made simultaneously and the bug disappeared — the correct answer is that you cannot know which change was responsible.
- **`git bisect` complexity** comes up frequently: 1024 commits → 10 rounds, 1 million commits → 20 rounds. The formula is ceil(log₂(n)).
- **Heisenbug recognition**: if a bug disappears when you add logging or run in debug mode, suspect timing — race conditions, event loop ordering, or timeout thresholds.
- **'I cannot reproduce it'** is the start of the investigation, not the end. Document the conditions under which it was reported, what environment it occurred in, and design experiments to increase frequency.
- **Regression tests have ROI**: the average production bug costs hours of engineering time, stakeholder communication, incident reports, and lost user trust. A fifteen-minute regression test amortizes that cost over every future refactoring forever.

items: **Reproduce first** — build the smallest, most isolated case that reliably triggers the bug before touching any code; a reliable reproduction is half the fix and makes the root cause obvious.
**The scientific method**: state a specific, falsifiable hypothesis; design an experiment that could prove it wrong; change only one thing at a time; update your model based on the result.

**Bisection** — `git bisect` finds the first bad commit in O(log n) steps; the same binary search logic applied mid-code (add a checkpoint at the midpoint, check if output is correct there, recurse into the failing half) isolates any pipeline bug efficiently.

**Rubber duck debugging** works because articulating code forces implicit assumptions to become explicit — the contradiction between intent and implementation surfaces in the act of explanation, often mid-sentence.

**Breakpoints and structured logging** are complementary: breakpoints for interactive local debugging with full state inspection; structured logs with correlation IDs for production systems where attaching a debugger is impossible.

**Defensive guard clauses and assertions** make assumptions executable — they convert silent wrong-state bugs ('Cannot read property of undefined') into loud, informative errors that name the violated assumption and its location.

**Every fixed bug earns a regression test** — encode the minimal reproduction as an automated check; this permanently prevents the bug from silently reappearing after future refactorings or dependency changes.

quiz.question: What is the most important first step when encountering a bug?
options: Open the debugger and set a breakpoint at the top of the file
Search Stack Overflow for the exact error message
Reproduce the bug reliably with the smallest possible failing case
Roll back the most recent commit and check if the bug disappears
quiz.explanation: You cannot fix what you cannot reliably trigger. A minimal reproduction isolates the bug from unrelated complexity and often reveals the cause immediately — before any other tooling is needed. It also gives you a clear pass/fail criterion for verifying the fix.

quiz.question: You form the hypothesis: 'the cart total is wrong because qty arrives as a string from the API.' What makes this a GOOD debugging hypothesis?
options: It is broad enough to cover many possible causes
It is specific and falsifiable — a single log statement can confirm or refute it
It was suggested by a senior engineer who has seen this before
It identifies the fix (coerce qty) rather than just the cause
quiz.explanation: A good hypothesis is specific and falsifiable: 'console.log(typeof item.qty)' will print either 'string' or 'number', immediately confirming or refuting it. Broad hypotheses cannot be tested efficiently. Identifying the fix is a next step — you first need to confirm the diagnosis.

quiz.question: You know a bug was introduced somewhere between commit A (working) and commit Z (broken) — 512 commits apart. What is the minimum number of test runs needed to find the first bad commit using git bisect?
quiz.explanation: git bisect performs binary search: ceil(log₂(512)) = ceil(9) = 9 rounds. Each round halves the remaining search space. 512 → 256 → 128 → 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 bad commit identified.

quiz.question: Why does rubber duck debugging work even though the duck provides no feedback?
options: Explaining forces you to slow down and re-read every line carefully
The act of articulating code makes implicit assumptions explicit, surfacing contradictions between intent and implementation
Talking activates a different hemisphere of the brain that is better at spotting errors
The duck's presence makes the programmer more accountable and focused
quiz.explanation: When writing code, the brain fills in intent automatically. When explaining to someone else, you must translate intent into explicit language — 'I assume this is always a string' — which forces you to question assumptions you did not know you were making. The contradiction between what you believe and what the code does surfaces in the act of articulation.

quiz.question: In a step debugger, what is the difference between Step Over and Step Into?
options: Step Over runs the program to completion; Step Into pauses at the next line
Step Over executes the current line without entering any called function; Step Into descends into the called function
Step Over skips the current line; Step Into executes it
Step Over is for loops; Step Into is for conditionals
quiz.explanation: Step Over treats a function call as a single step — the called function runs fully and you pause at the next line in the current scope. Step Into descends into the called function so you can inspect its internal execution. Use Step Over for functions you trust; Step Into only when you need to verify a function's behavior.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a guard clause at the entry of a function?
options: To improve performance by short-circuiting expensive operations
To satisfy TypeScript's strict mode compiler requirements
To catch precondition violations immediately with descriptive error messages, rather than allowing bad state to propagate silently
To prevent the function from being called with too many arguments
quiz.explanation: Without guards, a null or wrong-type argument propagates through several call layers before causing a cryptic error far from its origin. A guard catches the violation immediately at the point of entry and emits a message that names the violated assumption — drastically narrowing the search space during debugging.

quiz.question: A bug disappears when you add a console.log statement and reappears when you remove it. What is the most likely cause?
options: The console.log is accidentally fixing a variable assignment
The JavaScript engine optimizes the code differently when console is accessed
The bug is timing-dependent — likely a race condition or event-loop ordering issue — and the log statement changes execution timing
The bug only occurs in production builds which minify console calls away
quiz.explanation: A bug that disappears when observed is called a Heisenbug. Adding console.log is synchronous and changes the timing between asynchronous operations, which can hide or fix race conditions. Fix strategy: use non-intrusive logging that does not alter timing, or use tools designed for concurrent debugging.

quiz.question: In a production system with no attached debugger, which approach best provides visibility into a failing request's lifecycle?
options: Add alert() calls and deploy to see what fires in the browser
Structured logging with a correlation ID propagated through all services, with log-level controls via environment variable
Restart the service repeatedly until the bug reproduces in a dev environment
Wrap every function in a try-catch that logs the error and returns undefined
quiz.explanation: Structured logging with a correlation ID lets you filter your log aggregation tool by a single request and see its complete lifecycle across all services. Log levels (controlled by environment variable) let you enable debug verbosity temporarily without code changes or redeployment. This is the standard production debugging approach.

quiz.question: You have a four-step data pipeline (parse → validate → transform → render) that produces wrong output. How does the binary search technique apply?
options: Run all four steps and compare the final output to the expected output
Read all four step functions top-to-bottom looking for the error
Add a checkpoint assertion after step 2; if correct there, bug is in step 3 or 4; if wrong, bug is in step 1 or 2; recurse
Replace each step with a stub and add them back one at a time until the bug appears
quiz.explanation: Binary search: add a checkpoint at the midpoint (after step 2). If the intermediate output is correct, the bug must be in the second half (steps 3-4). If wrong, it is in the first half (steps 1-2). One checkpoint eliminates half the pipeline. A second checkpoint in the surviving half narrows it to one step. This is O(log n) vs O(n) for reading everything.

quiz.question: What is the most important reason to write a regression test immediately after fixing a bug?
options: It satisfies the code coverage requirement in the CI pipeline
It documents the root cause in a format that other developers can read
It permanently encodes the bug's triggering condition as an automated check, so any future change that reintroduces the bug fails loudly in CI rather than silently in production
It proves to the code reviewer that you tested the fix manually
quiz.explanation: A regression test's value is not in catching the bug the first time — you already did that manually. Its value is in future protection: any refactoring, dependency upgrade, or new feature that reintroduces the bug turns a green test red immediately, catching it in seconds at zero cost rather than in a production incident hours later.
